title_prefix: Trickled announcements are flushed in FI
mechanism: Core builds a vector of iterators over the pending set, heap-sorts it with CompareInvMempoolOrder and pops the top element until broadcast_max is reached (refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:6031-6086). The comparator (:5670-5684) delegates to m_mempool->CompareMiningScoreWithTopology, i.e. mining score with topology preserved -- at d3056bc this is the cluster-mempool ordering, not a plain ancestor feerate -- and Core's own comment at :6040-6041 states the purpose: 'Topologically and fee-rate sort the inventory we send for privacy and priority reasons.' The heap means the broadcast_max cut keeps the most valuable announcements. Ours (src/networking/protocol.lisp:3027-3072) pops the queue front until +inv-broadcast-target+ = 70 entries have been sent, so the drain is strictly FIFO and the tail past 70 waits for the next flush regardless of what it pays.
consequence: Two costs, both bounded. Priority: whenever a peer's queue exceeds 70, a high-feerate announcement queued behind cheap ones is delayed by whole flush intervals -- about 2 s per flush outbound and 5 s inbound, times the number of full flushes ahead of it -- so during exactly the fee spike where fast propagation matters most, our announcement order is the opposite of Core's. Privacy: our inv order is arrival order, which leaks the sequence in which transactions reached us; Core deliberately normalises to mempool order so an observer learns nothing from the ordering. Insertion order is already topological (a parent is accepted, and so relayed, before its child), so no orphan is created at the receiving peer by the current behaviour and nothing is lost -- the deferred announcements go out on the next flush. Bounded latency plus an ordering side channel, no lever a peer can drive: S3.
evidence: Probe ga11-txrelay-flush-order (scripts/dev.sh load + eval), warm image bitcoin-lisp-sbcl:2.6.5-4, raw send-message capture parsed back through bl.ser:parse-inv-payload. (1) Control, a queue shorter than the target: (:MESSAGES 1 :HASHES (1 2 3) :QUEUE-LEFT 0) -- the flush goes out as one inv in insertion order and empties the queue, so the capture and the ordering readout are both live. (2) The finding: 70 announcements at 1 sat/vB queued first, then one at 1000 sat/vB, then a single flush -- (:FLUSH-TARGET 70 :ANNOUNCED-THIS-FLUSH 70 :FIRST-ANNOUNCED-INDEX 10 :LAST-ANNOUNCED-INDEX 79 :HIGH-FEERATE-TX-ANNOUNCED NIL :HIGH-FEERATE-TX-STILL-QUEUED T :QUEUE-LEFT 1). The flush emitted exactly the first 70 in insertion order and deferred the one transaction worth a thousand times more; Core's heap would have popped it first. Ours: src/networking/protocol.lisp:2854, :3027-3072. Core at d3056bc: refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:5670-5684, :6031-6086.
fix_shape: Sort the pending announcements by mempool order before the per-flush cut, as Core does, rather than changing how they are stored on the way in. In %flush-peer-tx-invs, when the queue is longer than the flush target, order the candidates by the mempool's mining-score-with-topology comparator and take the top ones; a full sort of the queue is wasteful for the common case, so mirror Core's std::make_heap plus repeated pop_heap, which only orders as many entries as are actually sent. The comparator has to come from the mempool, so the flush needs the mempool it is already passed to remain non-NIL on the real path, and it must be the same ordering the miner uses so topology is preserved -- our cluster-mempool linearization is the natural source, and using a plain fee-rate instead would break the parent-before-child property that FIFO gives us for free today. This is best done together with the queue-representation change of finding 98f80da8, since both want the pending set to stop being a plain list: one structure that supports cheap insertion, no truncation, and an ordered drain satisfies both, and doing them separately means rewriting the same code twice.
